title: Treasury and Cash Management
outcomes: Explain treasury functions and motives for holding cash.
Explain techniques for managing collections, payments and float.

meta.exam_tip: In cash budgets, build a receipts table by month first; payments follow the same logic.

concepts.title: Treasury management and motives for holding cash
body: Treasury management handles cash, liquidity, funding, investment of surplus funds, foreign exchange and interest-rate risks, and banking relationships.

Motives for holding cash (Keynes): transaction (day-to-day payments), precautionary (unexpected needs) and speculative (taking advantage of opportunities). Banks may also require compensating balances.

Objectives: meet payment obligations on time while minimising idle balances; invest surpluses in safe, liquid instruments such as treasury bills, commercial paper, certificates of deposit and liquid funds.
concepts.analogy: Cash is needed to pay bills, but idle cash earns nothing — treasury balances the two.
concepts.work: A company parks month-end surpluses in an overnight liquid fund instead of a current account.

concepts.title: Cash budgets
body: A cash budget forecasts receipts and payments for each sub-period to show surpluses and shortages in advance. Methods: receipts and payments method (most common), adjusted profit and loss method, and balance sheet method.

Receipts: cash sales, collections from debtors (by lag pattern), other income; payments: purchases (by credit terms), wages, overheads (cash part), capital expenditure, taxes, dividends. Depreciation and other non-cash items are excluded.
Shortages are covered by arranging finance; surpluses are invested.
concepts.analogy: A cash budget is the calendar of money in and out.
concepts.work: Sales in March collected in April appear as April receipts.

concepts.title: Optimum cash balance: Baumol and Miller–Orr
body: Baumol model treats cash like inventory: optimum conversion size C = √(2U × P ÷ S), where U is annual cash requirement, P the cost per conversion and S the interest rate on securities. Total cost = (U ÷ C) × P + (C ÷ 2) × S.

Miller–Orr model allows random daily cash flows: Spread = 3 × (¾ × transaction cost × variance ÷ interest rate per day)^(1/3); upper limit = lower limit + spread; return point = lower limit + spread ÷ 3.
Other approaches: cash planning and cash budgets, and the Stone model (using forecasts to decide whether to act at limits).
concepts.analogy: Baumol suits steady cash use; Miller–Orr suits unpredictable swings.
concepts.work: Higher interest rates lower the optimum cash balance in both models.

concepts.title: Techniques of cash management
body: Speeding collections: concentration banking, lock-box systems, electronic transfers (NEFT, RTGS, UPI), prompt billing, and cash discounts.
Slowing payments ethically: pay on the due date, centralised payments, and using float (the gap between when a cheque is issued and when it is cleared).

Managing float: disbursement float (helpful to payer) and collection float (harmful); net float = disbursement float − collection float. Electronic payments have reduced float in India. Virtual accounts and cash pooling help corporate groups.
concepts.analogy: Get money in faster and let it go out on time — not earlier.
concepts.work: A dealer network paying through UPI cuts collection float to near zero.

illustrations.title: How much cash to draw each time?
illustrations.q: A firm needs ₹24 lakh of cash evenly over the year. Each conversion of securities into cash costs ₹300; securities earn 10%. Using Baumol's model find the optimum conversion size, number of conversions and total cost.

solution.text: At the optimum, transaction cost equals holding (opportunity) cost.

illustrations.title: Cash that swings daily
illustrations.q: Minimum cash balance ₹10,000; cost per transaction ₹50; variance of daily cash flows ₹40,00,000; daily interest rate 0.025%. Using Miller–Orr, find the spread, upper limit and return point.

solution.text: When cash hits the upper limit, buy securities to bring it down to the return point; when it hits the lower limit, sell securities to restore it to the return point.

jobs.title: Weekly cash forecast
jobs.situation: The CFO wants to know if a ₹2 crore tax payment next week needs a borrowing.
steps: Arrange a short-term line or liquidate investments if needed.
jobs.takeaway: Short-horizon forecasts prevent costly last-minute borrowing.

mcqs.q: Cash held to meet unexpected needs is for the:
mcqs.explain: Precautionary balances act as a cushion. In practice: often held in liquid investments.

mcqs.q: Which item is excluded from a cash budget?
mcqs.explain: Depreciation is non-cash. In practice: capital payments are included when paid.

mcqs.q: Under Baumol, if interest rates rise, the optimum cash conversion size:
mcqs.explain: Interest is in the denominator. In practice: higher returns on securities favour smaller balances.

mcqs.topic: Optimum cash balance: Baumol and Miller–Orr

mcqs.q: In Miller–Orr, the return point equals:
mcqs.explain: The return point is one-third of the spread above the lower limit. In practice: actions occur only at limits.

mcqs.q: A lock-box system is used to:
mcqs.explain: Customers pay into post boxes cleared by banks, reducing mail and processing float. In practice: replaced largely by electronic collections.

options: Time between issuing a cheque and its clearing
mcqs.explain: It lets the payer use funds a little longer. In practice: electronic payments shrink it.
The square-root formula balances the two costs. In practice: use as a check.

summary: Cash budget: receipts and payments; no non-cash items.

remember: Use daily interest and variance in Miller–Orr.

viva.q: Name the three motives for holding cash.
Why is a cash budget prepared?
viva.model: To forecast surpluses and shortages period by period so that financing or investment can be arranged in advance.
Optimum cash equals the square root of two times annual cash need times cost per conversion, divided by the interest rate.
Only when cash reaches the upper or lower limit, bringing it back to the return point by buying or selling securities.
Collecting payments at local branches and transferring surpluses quickly to a central account to reduce collection time.

cases.title: Pinnacle Retail
cases.case: Pinnacle Retail's sales: April ₹40 lakh, May ₹50 lakh, June ₹60 lakh; 25% cash, 75% collected the following month (March sales ₹36 lakh). Purchases are 60% of next month's sales, paid in the month of purchase. Opening cash on 1 April ₹5 lakh.

mcqs.explain: Cash 25% × 40 = 10 + 75% × 36 = 27 → 37. In practice: track by month.
60% of May sales 50 = 30. In practice: purchases lead sales.

mcqs.q: Closing cash on 30 April (₹ lakh), ignoring other items:
mcqs.explain: 5 + 37 − 30 = 12. In practice: add wages and other costs in reality.

mcqs.q: Surplus cash is best kept in:
mcqs.explain: Treasury invests surpluses safely and liquidly. In practice: liquid funds or T-bills.
